source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΡΗΘΕΙΣΑ ΕΝ ΛΙΜΩ ΚΑΙ ΑΥΧΜΩ. Λέων ἐρεύξεται, καὶ τίς οὐ φοβηθήσεται; Κύ ριος ὁ Θεὸς ἐλάλησε, καὶ τίς οὐ προφητεύσει; Προφητικὸν ποιήσωμεν τὸ τοῦ λόγου προοίμιον, καὶ τὸν θεοφορούμενον Ἀμὼς συνεργὸν εἰς τὴν τῶν προ κειμένων χρείαν παραλάβωμεν, τὰ ὅμοια τῶν ἡμῖν διοχλούντων κακῶν θεραπεύσαντα πάθη· τὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν συμφερόντων βουλήν τε καὶ γνώμην ἐκτιθέμενοι. Καὶ γὰρ αὐτὸς ὁ προφήτης ἐν τῇ φορᾷ τῶν ἀνω τέρω χρόνων, τοῦ λαοῦ καταλιπόντος τὴν πατρῴαν εὐσέβειαν, καὶ πατήσαντος μὲν τὴν τῶν νόμων ἀκρί βειαν, εἰς δὲ τὴν τῶν εἰδώλων θεραπείαν ὑπολισθήσαντος, κῆρυξ ἐγένετο μετανοίας· τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν παραινῶν, καὶ τῶν τιμωριῶν προφέρων τὴν ἀπειλήν. Ἐμοὶ δὲ δι' εὐχῆς ἀγέσθω τὸ μέχρι μέν τινος τῷ ζήλῳ τῆς παλαιᾶς ἱστορίας προσχρῆσθαι. Μηκέτι μέντοι καὶ τὴν ἔκβασιν τῶν τότε γενομένων ἰδεῖν ἀκόλουθον. Ἀπειθήσας γὰρ ὁ λαὸς, καὶ ὥσπερ πῶλος σκληρὸς καὶ δυσήνιος ἐνδακὼν τὸν χαλινὸν, οὐχ εἱλκύσθη πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον· ἐκτραπεὶς δὲ τῆς εὐθείας, τοσοῦτον ἔδραμεν ἄτακτα, καὶ τοῦ ἡνιόχου κατεφρυάξατο, μέχρις οὗ, τοῖς βαράθροις καὶ τοῖς κρημνοῖς ἐκπεσὼν, ἀξίαν τῆς δυσπειθείας τὴν πανωλεθρίαν ὑπέμεινεν. Ὃ μὴ γένοιτο νῦν ἐφ' ἡμῶν, παῖδες ἐμοὶ, οὓς διὰ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου ἐγέννησα, οὓς διὰ τῆς εὐλογίας τῶν χειρῶν ἐσπαργάνωσα. Ἀλλ' ἔστω ἀκοὴ εὐγνώμων, ψυχὴ εὐπειθὴς, ἁπαλῶς δεχομένη τὰς παραινέσεις, εἴκουσα τῷ λέγοντι, ὡς κηρὸς τῷ σφρα γίζοντι, ἵνα διὰ μιᾶς ταύτης σπουδῆς κἀγὼ λάβω καρπὸν τῶν πονουμένων εὐφραίνοντα, καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐν καιρῷ τῆς ἀπαλλαγῆς τῶν δεινῶν τὴν γενομένην παραίνεσιν ἐπαινέσητε. Τί οὖν ἐστιν ὅπερ ἐνδείκνυται μὲν ὁ λόγος, ἔτι δὲ μετεώρους κατέχει τὰς ψυ χὰς τῇ ἐλπίδι τῆς ἀκοῆς, βραδύνων δημοσιεύειν τὸ προσδοκώμενον; Οὐρανὸν ὁρῶμεν, ἀδελφοὶ, στεγανὸν, γυμνὸν, καὶ ἀνέφελον, στυγνὴν ἐμποιοῦντα τὴν αἰθρίαν ταύτην, καὶ καταλυποῦντα τῇ καθαρότητι, ἣν λίαν ἐπ εθυμοῦμεν τὸ πρῶτον, ἡνίκα ἂν, ἐπὶ πολὺ σκεπασθεὶς τοῖς νέφεσι, ζοφώδεις ἡμᾶς καὶ ἀνηλίους εἰργάσατο. Γῆ δὲ καταξηρανθεῖσα εἰς ἄκρον ἀηδὴς μέν ἐστιν ὀφθῆναι, στείρα δὲ πρὸς γεωργίαν καὶ ἄγονος, εἰς σχίσματα διαῤῥαγεῖσα, καὶ εἰς τὸ βάθος δεχομένη καταλάμπουσαν τὴν ἀκτῖνα. Πηγαὶ δὲ ἡμᾶς ἐπέλιπον πλούσιαί τε καὶ ἀένναοι, καὶ ποταμῶν με γάλων ἐδαπανήθη τὰ ῥεύματα, παῖδες δὲ αὐτὰ σμικρότατοι καταπεζεύουσι, καὶ γυναῖκες περαιοῦνται μετὰ φορτίων· τοὺς δὲ πολλοὺς ἡμῶν καὶ τὸ ποτὸν ἐπέλειψε, καὶ ἐν ἀπορίᾳ τοῦ ζῇν καθεστήκαμεν. Ἰσραηλῖται νέοι, Μωϋσῆν ζητοῦντες νέον, καὶ ῥάβδον θαυμασίων ποιητικὴν, ἵνα πάλιν πέτραι πλη γεῖσαι τὴν χρείαν τοῦ διψῶντος λαοῦ θεραπεύσωσι, νεφέλαι δὲ παράδοξοι τροφὴν ἀσυνήθη τὸ μάννα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις καταψεκάσωσιν. Εὐλαβηθῶμεν μὴ γενώμεθα τοῖς ὀψιγόνοις καινὸν ἐπὶ λιμοῦ καὶ τιμω ρίας διήγημα. Εἶδον τὰς ἀρούρας, καὶ πολλὰ κατ εδάκρυσα τῆς ἀκαρπίας αὐτῶν· καὶ ἐξέχεα θρῆνον, ἐπειδὴ μὴ ὑετὸς ἐφ' ἡμᾶς ἐξεχύθη. Τὰ μὲν τῶν σπερμάτων πρὸ τῆς ἐκβολῆς ἐξηράνθη, ταῖς βώλοις τοιαῦτα μείναντα οἷα τὸ ἄροτρον ἔκρυψε· τὰ δὲ μικρὸν προκύψαντα καὶ βλαστήσαντα ἐλεεινῶς ἀπεμαράνθη τῷ καύματι· ὡς νῦν εὐκαίρως τινὰ τὴν εὐαγγελικὴν ἀναστρέψαι φωνὴν, λέγοντα· Οἱ μὲν ἐργάται πολλοὶ, τὸ δὲ θέρος οὐδ' ὀλίγον.
thought_title: Opening appeal: let us hear like wax, for the drought is God's warning
orientation: Basil opens his homily by invoking the prophet Amos as a fellow herald of repentance, then describes the drought's devastation and urges his hearers to receive his counsel obediently.
pass_a_gloss: A homily delivered in famine and drought. A lion will roar, and who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy? Let us make the opening of the discourse prophetic, and let us take the God-inspired Amos as a fellow worker for the need of the matters set before us, since he healed sufferings similar to the evils troubling us; setting forth the counsel and judgment concerning what is beneficial. For indeed this very prophet, in the course of the times above, when the people had abandoned the ancestral piety, and had trampled the exactness of the laws, and had slipped away into the service of idols, became a herald of repentance; urging the turning back, and bringing forward the threat of punishments. But let it be led by prayer for me to make use of the zeal of the old history up to a point. No longer, however, to see also the outcome of the things that happened then as following. For the people disobeyed, and like a hard and unbridled colt biting the bit, was not drawn toward what is beneficial; and turning aside from the straight way, ran so much in disorder, and snorted against the charioteer, until, falling out into pits and cliffs, it endured total destruction worthy of its disobedience. May this not happen now upon us, my children, whom I begot through the Gospel, whom I swaddled through the blessing of the hands. But let there be a well-disposed hearing, an obedient soul, receiving the exhortations softly, yielding to the speaker, as wax to the one sealing, so that through this one eagerness I too may receive fruit of my labors that gladdens, and you in the time of release from the terrors may praise the exhortation that was made. What then is it which the discourse indicates, and still holds the souls suspended in hope of the hearing, delaying to publish what is expected? We see the sky, brothers, close-covered, bare, and cloudless, producing this gloomy clear weather, and grieving by the clarity, which we very much desired at first, whenever, having been covered for a long time by the clouds, it made us dark and sunless. And the earth, dried up to the extreme, is unpleasant to look at, barren for farming and unfruitful, broken apart into fissures, and receiving into its depth the shining ray. And the springs failed us, rich and ever-flowing, and the streams of great rivers were consumed, and very small children cross them on foot, and women cross over with loads; and for most of us even drink failed, and we stand in lack of the means of living. Young Israelites, seeking a new Moses, and a rod that works wonders, so that again rocks struck may heal the need of the thirsty people, and marvelous clouds may rain down unusual food, the manna, upon humans. Let us beware lest we become for later generations a new tale of famine and punishment. I saw the fields, and I wept much over their unfruitfulness; and I poured out lamentation, since rain was not poured out upon us. Some of the seeds dried up before sprouting, remaining in the clods such as the plow hid them; and others, having come up a little and sprouted, were pitifully withered by the burning heat; so that now someone may fittingly reverse the Gospel saying, saying: The workers are many, but the harvest is not even a little.

choices.term: ἐν τῇ φορᾷ τῶν ἀνωτέρω χρόνων
choices.english: in the course of the times above
choices.why: Keeps the temporal sense of φορά as a sweep or course of time, and ἀνωτέρω as 'above' (earlier), matching Basil's framing of the old history.
rejected: in the rush of earlier times
in the flow of ancient days

choices.term: ὥσπερ πῶλος σκληρὸς καὶ δυσήνιος ἐνδακὼν τὸν χαλινὸν
choices.english: like a hard and unbridled colt biting the bit
choices.why: Preserves the vivid equine image and the active participle 'biting' as the colt's resistance, not a passive state.
rejected: like a stubborn and unmanageable colt that bit the bridle

choices.term: ἁπαλῶς δεχομένη τὰς παραινέσεις, εἴκουσα τῷ λέγοντι, ὡς κηρὸς τῷ σφραγίζοντι
choices.english: receiving the exhortations softly, yielding to the speaker, as wax to the one sealing
choices.why: Keeps the wax-seal simile literal and the participles as active qualities of the soul Basil hopes for.
rejected: gently accepting the advice, giving way to the speaker like wax to a seal

choices.why: Renders the paradoxical description literally: στεγανός means covered or close, yet the sky is also bare and cloudless, which Basil uses to describe the oppressive clear weather.
Keeps the oxymoron of 'gloomy clear weather' (στυγνὴν αἰθρίαν), which is Basil's point: the very clarity they once wanted now grieves them.
rejected: causing this clear sky to be dismal

choices.why: Renders the verb literally: children go on foot across the riverbeds, emphasizing how low the water has fallen.

bible_refs.note: Λέων ἐρεύξεται, καὶ τίς οὐ φοβηθήσεται; Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἐλάλησε, καὶ τίς οὐ προφητεύσει;

pass_b_english: A lion roars, and who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy? (Amos 3:8). Let us make the opening of this discourse prophetic, and let us take the God-inspired Amos as our partner for the need before us, since he healed sufferings like the evils now troubling us. We set out his counsel and judgment about what is beneficial. For this same prophet, in the course of the times above, when the people had abandoned their ancestral piety, trampled the exactness of the laws, and slipped away into the worship of idols, became a herald of repentance: urging them to turn back, and holding before them the threat of punishments.

For my part, let it be granted by prayer that I may draw on the old history as an example up to a point—but may I no longer see the outcome of what happened then follow in the same way. For the people disobeyed, and like a hard and unbridled colt biting the bit, they were not drawn toward what was beneficial. They turned aside from the straight road and ran so wildly, and snorted against the charioteer, until they fell into pits and over cliffs and endured total destruction as the worthy reward of their disobedience. May that not happen now among us, my children, whom I have begotten through the Gospel, whom I have swaddled through the blessing of my hands.

But let there be a receptive ear, a compliant soul, receiving the exhortations softly, yielding to the speaker, as wax to the one sealing—so that through this one effort I may receive a fruit that gladdens my labors, and you may praise the exhortation given when the time of deliverance from these terrors comes.

What then is it that the discourse points to, but still holds your souls suspended in hope of hearing, delaying to make public what is expected? We see the sky, brothers: impervious, bare, and cloudless, producing this gloomy clear weather, and grieving us by the very clarity that we once desired so much, when it was covered for a long time with clouds and made us dark and sunless. The earth, dried up to the extreme, is unpleasant to look at, barren for farming and unfruitful, split into cracks and receiving the blazing ray into its depths. The rich and ever-flowing springs have failed us, and the streams of great rivers have been used up. The smallest children trample them underfoot, and women pass over with their loads. For most of us even drinking water has failed, and we stand in perplexity about how to live.

Young Israelites seek a new Moses and a rod that works wonders, so that rocks may be struck again and heal the need of the thirsty people, and marvelous clouds may rain down unaccustomed food—manna—upon human beings. Let us beware lest we become a new story for later generations about famine and punishment.

I saw the fields, and I wept much over their barrenness. I poured out lamentation, because no rain was poured out upon us. Some of the seeds dried up before they sprouted, remaining in the clods just as the plow had hidden them. Others, after peeping out a little and sprouting, were pitifully withered by the burning heat. So now one might fittingly reverse the Gospel saying: The workers are many, but the harvest is not even a little (Matthew 9:37).

problems.ruling: στεγανόν means watertight/impermeable; 'close-covered' loses the drought-relevant sense.

problems.quote: Small children cross them on foot
problems.why: καταπεζεύουσι means 'trample them underfoot' (the rivers are so dried up), not 'cross them on foot' which implies traversing.
problems.fix: and the smallest children trample them underfoot
problems.ruling: καταπεζεύουσι = 'trample underfoot' (dried riverbeds), not 'cross on foot'—misleads reader.

problems.quote: I may make use of the zeal of the old history
problems.source_quote: τῷ ζήλῳ τῆς παλαιᾶς ἱστορίας προσχρῆσθαι
problems.why: ζῆλος here means 'narrative/record' (the history itself), not 'zeal'; προσχρῆσθαι means 'to use as an example/addition'.
problems.fix: I may draw on the old history as an example
problems.ruling: ζῆλος = 'zeal', not 'narrative'; but English says 'zeal of history'—odd but not mistranslation. Not major.

last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν συμφερόντων βουλήν τε καὶ γνώμην ἐκτιθέμενοι
last_rejected.why: Source says 'setting out the counsel and opinion about beneficial things'; English drops the method/attitude and adds 'his judgment'.
last_rejected.fix: setting out the counsel and opinion about what is beneficial
last_rejected.ruling: 'Judgment' is within γνώμη's range; 'setting out' and 'we set out' both convey ἐκτιθέμενοι adequately.

last_rejected.quote: since he healed sufferings like the evils now troubling us.
last_rejected.source_quote: τὰ ὅμοια τῶν ἡμῖν διοχλούντων κακῶν θεραπεύσαντα πάθη
last_rejected.why: Source says Amos healed sufferings like the evils now troubling us; 'since' misreads the participle as causal rather than appositional.
last_rejected.fix: who healed sufferings like the evils now troubling us
last_rejected.ruling: The participle θεραπεύσαντα is causal/attributive; 'since' correctly captures why Amos is taken as partner.

last_rejected.source_quote: Οἱ μὲν ἐργάται πολλοί, τὸ δὲ θέρος οὐδ' ὀλίγον
last_rejected.why: Basil explicitly reverses the Gospel saying; the source verse is Matthew 9:37/Luke 10:2, but Basil's reversed form does not match the standard citation. The standard verse says 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few'—Basil has inverted both pairs. The citation should note this inversion or cite the adapted form.
last_rejected.ruling: Matthew 9:37 is the correct source; Basil's inversion is visible in the English itself. No reference error.

last_rejected.why: στεγανὸν means 'tight, compact, watertight' or 'cloudless' in context; 'impervious' suggests resistant to penetration, which misleads about the sky's quality—it's sealed against rain, not impervious in the modern sense.
last_rejected.ruling: στεγανὸν means watertight/impervious; 'impervious' correctly renders the sky sealed against rain.
